name: Bupivacaine
route_note: local infiltration, peripheral nerve block, epidural and spinal injection; liposomal form for infiltration

discovery.note: Synthesised as a long-acting butyl-substituted analogue of mepivacaine; clinical use began in the early 1960s.

tagline: Long-acting local anaesthetic for spinal, epidural and nerve-block anaesthesia
summary: Bupivacaine is a long-acting amide local anaesthetic that blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in nerves. It is widely used for spinal and epidural anaesthesia, labour analgesia and nerve blocks. It is more cardiotoxic than lidocaine, and accidental intravascular injection can cause cardiac arrest, which lipid emulsion therapy can treat.
mechanism: Bupivacaine crosses the nerve membrane in its uncharged form and, once protonated inside the axon, binds the inner pore of voltage-gated sodium channels, preferentially in open and inactivated states. This prevents depolarisation and conduction of action potentials.

Small pain and autonomic fibres are blocked before large motor fibres, especially at low concentrations, allowing epidural analgesia with limited motor block. High lipid solubility and protein binding give a long duration, but slow dissociation from cardiac sodium channels underlies its arrhythmogenic potential.
uses: Local infiltration and postsurgical analgesia (including liposomal formulation)

history.title: Clinical introduction
history.detail: First clinical reports describe it as a long-acting local anaesthetic.

history.title: Cardiotoxicity warning
history.detail: George Albright's editorial links bupivacaine and etidocaine to cardiac arrest after regional anaesthesia.

history.title: Obstetric restriction
history.detail: FDA advises against 0.75% bupivacaine for obstetric epidural anaesthesia after maternal deaths.

history.title: Lipid rescue
history.detail: Guy Weinberg shows lipid emulsion reverses bupivacaine cardiotoxicity in rats; the first human case is reported in 2006.

history.title: Liposomal bupivacaine
history.detail: FDA approves Exparel for postsurgical infiltration analgesia.

serious: local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (seizures, ventricular arrhythmias, cardiac arrest)
safety.boxed_warning: The 0.75% concentration is not recommended for obstetrical anaesthesia; cardiac arrest with difficult resuscitation or death has followed its use for epidural anaesthesia in obstetric patients.

facts: Levobupivacaine and ropivacaine, single S-enantiomers, were developed to reduce bupivacaine's cardiotoxicity.
